cards.title: Multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion

depth.text: Ruby patched **seven flaws** in text handling, some of which could let attackers **run code**

The flaws affect Ruby’s **regular-expression engine** and string case conversion; proof-of-concept code can trigger **remote code execution** for some of them. Fixes are in Ruby **4.0.10, 3.4.13, and 3.3.14**; Ruby 3.2 and earlier will not receive them.

The 1252 case conversion code doesn't handle this; it looks like it checks for headroom in the buffer…

cards.title: The x86 CPU: From 4004 to 486

depth.text: someone traced **x86's odd habits** back through the chips and **customers** that shaped them
The article traces **little-endian byte order** to the Datapoint 2200, and shows the 8086 giving 8080 registers homes in AX, BX, CX and DX so **assembly could be translated** line by line.

cards.camps: Two camps: the article says bit-serial arithmetic explains why the Datapoint stored low bytes first; a commenter says the original reason was the terminal's low-to-high address processing, with the arithmetic explanation becoming relevant on the 8080.

comments.text: Learned to program on an 8088 machine with Hercules mono graphics card, first in GW-Basic which was godawful, then in A86 assembler and finally Turbo Pascal which was a pinnacle of human engineering, a portal into a wonderful future ahead. There was great excitement and relief when the 80386 came out with its 32bit address linear memory model. Everything suddenly became possible - serious compute…

This is a neat history. However, going to be a bit nitpicky since they put this in bold re the 8008: "Intel did not design the instruction set of this chip" .. kinda true in a broad sense, but Intel engineers including Stan Mazor did change and enhance it, like adding increment and decrement operations and some other stuff mentioned in…
One thing I'd emphasize is that the 4004 is not related to the 8008 at all, except that many of the same people worked on both chips.

Cool article, thanks! Nitpick: the reason behind the little endianness _originally_ was data access speed-up on 2200, not arithmetic. The 2200 only had 8-bit arithmetic (as did 8008), but its address bus was processed low-to-high. The arithmetic angle became relevant in 8080, with its 16-bit arithmetic. Side benefit: casting between 8- and 16-bit data using the same address. Another nitpick: the…

The A20 gate is one of the most aggravating bits of x86 history. Not that they added it (backwards compatibility is very desirable for sales, so it makes sense that they added it), but that anyone was stupid enough to depend on that wrapping behavior in the first place. Such a short sighted, sloppy thing to do.

glossary.context window: The amount of text and information an AI can take into account at one time.
glossary.tokens: Small pieces of text an AI counts as it reads or writes; they can affect how much a request costs.
glossary.Pareto frontier: A set of choices where you can't get better on one measure without giving something up on another.
glossary.agent: An AI system that can take steps and use tools to get a task done, not just answer questions.
glossary.ACH: Automated Clearing House: a US system banks use to send money between accounts electronically.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.edge case: A situation outside the usual path that can make software behave differently or break.
glossary.comprehension debt: When a system is built or changed faster than the people working on it can understand it.
glossary.world model: An AI meant to represent a scene and how things in it change.
glossary.native audio: Sound made as part of the world that can change with what is happening in the scene.
glossary.panorama grounding: Using a 360-degree image as the starting point for a generated world.
glossary.object permanence: The idea that something stays where it is even when you cannot see it.
glossary.Elo: A score that estimates how strong a player is by comparing their wins and losses against other players.
glossary.orchestration: Coordinating several AI agents so they can hand tasks to one another.
glossary.tokens per second: A measure of how quickly a model produces text.
glossary.benchmark: A test people use to compare how well different tools do a task.
glossary.Agent Duel: A battle system on top of OpenCode where models compete.
glossary.regular expression: A text pattern that tells a program what kind of words or characters to look for.
glossary.remote code execution: A security flaw that lets someone run commands on another person's computer.
glossary.heap buffer overflow: A bug where a program writes past the space it set aside for data, possibly damaging nearby memory.
glossary.double free: A bug where a program marks the same piece of memory as free twice, which can confuse or crash it.
glossary.out-of-bounds read: A program reads data from beyond the area it was supposed to read.
glossary.PoC: Proof of Concept: a small demonstration that shows a bug can be triggered.
glossary.heap grooming: Arranging a program’s memory so a flaw is more likely to behave in a useful way for an attacker.
glossary.open-source: Software whose code is shared publicly so people can inspect it, change it, or build on it.
glossary.SSO: Single Sign-On: a way to use one sign-in for several work services.
glossary.Free/Busy: A calendar feature that shows when people, rooms, or other resources are available.
glossary.PPA: Power, performance and area: three things chip designers try to balance when improving a design.
glossary.RISC-V: A processor design that sets out the basic instructions software runs on.
glossary.RTL: Right-to-left: writing that runs from the right side of a line toward the left.
glossary.EDA: Electronic design automation: software engineers use to design and test chips.
glossary.ASIC: Application-specific integrated circuit: a chip built for a particular job.
glossary.FPGA: Field-programmable gate array: a chip that can be set up for different hardware jobs after it is made.
glossary.SIMD: Single Instruction, Multiple Data: a way to apply one operation to several values at once.
glossary.IP: Intellectual property: creative work, characters, or brands that a person or company can have legal rights over.
glossary.agent task: A job where an AI has to use tools and take several steps to get something done.
glossary.post-training: Extra training after a model's initial training that shapes how it responds.
glossary.reinforcement learning: A way to train an AI by rewarding choices that work and discouraging choices that do not.
glossary.pass@1: The share of test problems a model solves on its first try.
glossary.sandbox: A separate, contained space where software can be tested without affecting the rest of a computer or system.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.CMOS: Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor: a common way to make electronic parts, including memory chips.
glossary.KVM: Kernel-based Virtual Machine: a Linux feature for running virtual machines.
glossary.MMU: Memory Management Unit: hardware that helps an operating system manage memory and keep programs separate.
glossary.INIT: A processor startup signal that puts it into an initial state.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a standard ID assigned to a publicly known security flaw so people can refer to the same issue.
glossary.nested virtualization: Running a virtual machine inside another virtual machine.
glossary.unikernel: A way to build an application with only the operating-system pieces it needs, instead of relying on a full general-purpose system.
glossary.reverse engineering: Figuring out how a program works by examining the program itself.
glossary.binary: A program file a computer can run.
glossary.disassembler: A tool that turns a program’s machine instructions into a form people can inspect.
glossary.decompiler: A tool that turns a compiled program into code that is easier for people to read.
glossary.firmware: The built-in software that tells a device's hardware how to work.
glossary.hypothesis: A possible explanation that you test to see if it is true.
glossary.mDTC: micro–Data Transfer Cartridge: the name for the storage cartridge in the F-22 headline.
glossary.PCMCIA: Personal Computer Memory Card International Association: a name used for a removable-card format found in older computers and equipment.
glossary.CF: CompactFlash: a removable storage card used to move files between devices.
glossary.linear memory-mapped card: A storage card that lets a device read its memory directly, without a storage controller in between.
glossary.NOR flash: A kind of memory chip that keeps its contents even when the power is off.
glossary.SCIF: Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility: a secure room for handling classified information.
glossary.x86: A family of chip designs used in many personal computers.
glossary.little-endian: A way to store a multi-byte number with its lowest-value byte first.
glossary.bit-serial: A design that handles a number one bit at a time.
glossary.register: A small storage spot inside a processor that code can use while it runs.
glossary.IPO: Initial Public Offering: when a company first offers its shares for the public to buy.
glossary.Class A common stock: One category of a company’s ownership shares; a company may have other categories with different rules.
glossary.underwriters: Financial firms that help a company sell its shares to investors.
glossary.market cap: The total market value of a company’s shares.
glossary.exit liquidity: People who buy shares from someone trying to sell, making it easier for that seller to get out.
glossary.SaaS: Software as a Service: software you access over the internet, with the provider running it for you.
glossary.DRM: Digital Rights Management: restrictions in software that control how it can be copied or used.
glossary.vendor lock-in: When relying on a company’s tools makes it difficult to move to another company’s tools.
